title: Borrowing Basics
description: What borrowing costs, what secures a loan, and whether the payment fits.
wolfLine: Borrow the money. Read the leash before you sign.

debt.definition: Money you’ve borrowed and still have to pay back.
debt.example: You borrow $1,000 from a bank. You now have $1,000 of debt.

loan.definition: Money a lender gives you now, which you repay over time, usually with interest.
loan.example: A car loan: the bank pays for the car, you pay the bank back each month.

credit-card.definition: A card that lets you buy now and pay later. Whatever you don’t pay off each month gets charged interest.
credit-card.example: Buy a $500 TV on the card, pay $100 this month, and you’re charged interest on the other $400.

good-debt.definition: Cheap borrowing for something that builds your future, like a home or a skill that raises your pay.
good-debt.example: An affordable loan for training that gets you a better-paid job.

bad-debt.definition: Expensive borrowing for things that quickly lose their value.
bad-debt.example: A holiday paid for on a credit card you can’t pay off.

mortgage.definition: A big loan used to buy a home, usually paid back over 15 to 30 years.
mortgage.example: The bank lends you most of the price of a flat, and you repay it monthly.

principal.definition: The amount you borrowed, not counting interest.
principal.example: Borrow $2,400 for a laptop. The principal is $2,400.

secured-loan.definition: A loan backed by something the lender can take if you stop paying, such as a car.
secured-loan.example: A car loan: miss enough payments and the lender can take the car.

unsecured-loan.definition: A loan with no property behind it. The lender trusts you to pay, and charges more when that trust is thin.
unsecured-loan.example: Most credit cards and many personal loans are unsecured.

cosigner.definition: Someone who signs a loan with you and has to pay it if you do not.
cosigner.example: A parent co-signs a $4,000 loan. If you miss payments, the lender can collect from your parent.

lessons.title: What Is Debt?
lessons.summary: Borrowing, loans, and what it really costs.

steps.context: [[Debt]] is money you’ve borrowed and still have to pay back.
steps.prompt: You borrow $1,000 from a bank to buy a laptop. What do you now have?
steps.explain: Borrowed money isn’t yours to keep. It’s debt until you pay it back.

steps.context: A [[loan]] is one common way to borrow: a lender gives you money now, and you pay it back over time. You usually pay back **more** than you borrowed. The extra is [[interest]], and this time you’re the one paying it.
steps.prompt: You borrow $1,000 and pay back $1,100 in total. What’s the extra $100?
steps.explain: The price of using someone else’s money.

steps.context: A [[credit card]] lets you buy now and pay later. If you don’t pay the full bill each month, you’re charged interest on what’s left, and it’s usually a lot.
steps.prompt: You buy a $500 TV on a credit card and pay back $100 this month. What happens to the other $400?
steps.explain: Whatever you don’t pay off keeps costing you.

steps.context: Cheap borrowing that builds your future, like a home or a skill that raises your pay, is often called [[good debt]]. Expensive borrowing for things that quickly lose value is [[bad debt]].
steps.prompt: Which of these is closest to bad debt?
choices: A low-cost loan for training that raises your pay
A holiday on a credit card you can’t pay off
An affordable loan to buy a home
steps.explain: High interest, and the holiday is over long before the debt is.

steps.prompt: All debt is bad.
steps.explain: Cheap debt that builds your future can be a smart move. Expensive debt for fun rarely is.

steps.context: A [[mortgage]] is a big loan used to buy a home. People usually pay it back over 15 to 30 years.
steps.prompt: What is a mortgage for?
steps.explain: Homes cost too much to buy outright, so most people borrow.

steps.prompt: Recap: match each word to what it means.
pairs: Borrowed money you repay over time
A loan to buy a home
The extra you pay to borrow

lessons.title: What Borrowing Costs
lessons.summary: You pay back more than you borrowed. That gap is the price.

steps.context: [[Debt]] means you pay the money back. The extra on top is [[interest]], and this time you are the one paying it.
steps.prompt: You borrow $800 and pay back $920. What is the extra $120?
steps.explain: The extra is the price of the loan.

steps.prompt: You borrow $3,000 and pay back $3,450. How much interest did you pay?
If a friend lends you $200 and you pay back exactly $200, you paid no interest.
steps.explain: No extra money changed hands. You still owed the $200 until you paid it.

steps.prompt: Which borrowing is closest to good debt?
choices: A low-rate loan for training that raises your pay
A vacation on a card you cannot pay off
New shoes you do not need, financed for a year
why: A skill that raises your pay can outlast the loan.
High interest, and the trip is over.
The shoes wear out. The payments do not.
steps.explain: Cheap borrowing that builds your future can be worth it. The other two are expensive and gone fast.

steps.prompt: Why do lenders charge interest?
choices: They are paid for letting you use their money
The law says every loan costs 10%
steps.explain: Their money is busy working for you, so they charge rent on it.

steps.prompt: A $1,500 loan costs $180 in interest. How much do you pay back in total?

lessons.title: Principal and Interest
lessons.summary: One part is what you borrowed. The other part is the price.

steps.context: The [[principal]] is the amount you borrowed, not counting interest. Pay $2,200 back on a $2,000 loan and $200 of it is interest.
steps.prompt: You borrow $2,000. In loan words, what is that $2,000 called?
steps.explain: Principal is the amount you borrowed.

steps.prompt: Principal $4,000. You pay back $4,640. How much is interest?
Each month you pay $150. $110 of it cuts the principal. How much of the payment is interest?
Paying extra, above the required payment, usually cuts the principal faster.
steps.explain: Less principal left means less interest next time.

steps.prompt: Two loans, same principal. One charges more interest. Which costs more in total?
steps.explain: Same amount borrowed, higher price.

steps.prompt: The amount you borrowed, before interest, is the ___.
steps.explain: Principal first. Interest is the extra.

lessons.title: Secured or Unsecured
lessons.summary: Some loans have something to take. Some only have your promise.

steps.context: A [[secured loan]] is backed by something the lender can take, like the car. An [[unsecured loan]] has no property behind it. A typical [[credit card]] is unsecured, which is one reason its interest is often high.
steps.prompt: A car loan lets the lender take the car if you stop paying. What kind of loan is that?
steps.explain: The car is the backup.

steps.prompt: Secured or unsecured?
items: Car loan, and the lender can take the car
Loan for a boat, and the lender can take the boat
Personal loan with no property behind it

steps.prompt: An unsecured loan is always cheaper than a secured one.
steps.explain: No collateral usually means a higher rate, not a lower one.

steps.prompt: You stop paying a secured car loan. What can the lender do?
choices: Take the car and sell it
steps.explain: That is the deal you signed.

steps.prompt: Why might a lender offer a lower rate on a secured loan?
choices: They can take the property if you do not pay
Secured loans are illegal to price high
The rate is set by your birthday
steps.explain: Less risk for them, so they can charge less.

steps.prompt: Match each loan to what sits behind it.

lessons.title: The Loan Agreement
lessons.summary: The page you sign is the whole deal. Read it.

steps.context: A loan agreement is the written deal: how much you borrow, what you pay, and how long it lasts.

doc.title: Northline Credit Union
doc.subtitle: Personal loan agreement
doc.note: 24 payments of $115. Miss a payment and a late fee can be added.

steps.prompt: What is the principal on this agreement?
steps.explain: The amount borrowed: $2,400.

doc.title: Northline Credit Union
doc.subtitle: Personal loan agreement
doc.note: 24 payments of $115. Miss a payment and a late fee can be added.

steps.prompt: How much interest do you pay over the full 24 months?
steps.explain: The interest line: $360.

doc.title: Northline Credit Union
doc.subtitle: Personal loan agreement
doc.note: 24 payments of $115. Miss a payment and a late fee can be added.

steps.prompt: What do you pay back in total?
Check the monthly payment against the total. $2,760 ÷ 24 months equals?
Once you sign, a late payment can cost an extra fee on top of the payment.
steps.explain: The note says so. The payment is not the only number that matters.

steps.prompt: What should you know before you sign?
choices: The total you will pay, not just the monthly payment
steps.explain: The monthly number hides the $360.

lessons.title: Can You Afford the Payment?
lessons.summary: A payment that fits this month can still cost more overall.

steps.context: A payment you cannot cover after needs is a payment you cannot afford. Run the numbers before you sign.
steps.prompt: You bring home $2,800. Needs take $2,200. How much is left?
A loan wants $700 a month and you have $600 left after needs. What do you do?
choices: Do not take it. The payment does not fit
Take it. The lender would not offer it otherwise
steps.explain: If it does not fit, it is not affordable.

steps.prompt: Offer A: $200 × 36 payments. What do you pay in total?
Offer B: $140 × 60 payments. What do you pay in total?
How much more does Offer B cost than Offer A?
Both loans hand you $6,000. Which one costs less overall?
choices: Offer B, because the payment is smaller
why: Smaller each month, more in the end.
The totals on the two sheets do not match.
steps.explain: The smaller payment lasts longer and costs $1,200 more.

lessons.title: Co-signing
lessons.summary: Your name on someone else’s loan is your loan too.

steps.context: A [[co-signer|cosigner]] signs with the borrower and has to pay if the borrower does not. The loan can show on both credit records.
steps.prompt: You co-sign a friend’s $4,000 loan. They stop paying. What can the lender do?
choices: Nothing. You only wrote a reference
Take the debt off both of you
steps.explain: A co-signer agrees to pay.

steps.prompt: Co-signing is just a character reference. You cannot be made to pay.
steps.explain: It is a legal promise to pay the debt.

steps.prompt: The friend misses payments and $1,600 is still owed. You are the co-signer. How much can the lender ask you for?
steps.explain: The remaining $1,600. Co-signing means you owe it too.

steps.prompt: Your own loan application asks about debts. Does the co-signed loan count?
choices: Yes. Lenders treat it as your debt too
No. It is only the friend’s
steps.explain: It can use up room you needed for your own loan.

steps.prompt: When is co-signing least risky?
choices: When you can afford the full payment yourself, and you trust them to pay
When you have not read the agreement
steps.explain: Assume you might be the one paying.

steps.prompt: The friend pays the loan off on time. What was the cost to you?
choices: Maybe nothing in money, but your name was on the debt the whole time
steps.explain: The risk was real even though the bill never landed on you.

lessons.title: Leo’s First Loan
lessons.summary: A course that raises pay can still be a bad loan.

story.title: The first loan
story.body:
Leo wants a $2,000 certificate course that could raise his pay. The school offers a loan: **$2,000** now, then **24** payments of **$105**.

Leo brings home **$2,600** a month. Rent and other needs take **$2,150**. He has been late on a phone bill before, and his cousin offered to co-sign.

steps.prompt: How much interest does Leo pay over the full loan?
After needs, how much of Leo’s paycheck is left each month?
The payment is $105 and Leo has $450 left. Does the payment fit?
choices: No. $105 is more than he brings home
steps.explain: The payment fits. Fitting is not the same as being worth it.

steps.prompt: Leo has been late on bills. What is the risk if his cousin co-signs?
choices: His cousin has to pay if Leo falls behind
The cousin’s name is only a reference
steps.explain: Co-signing puts the cousin on the hook.

steps.prompt: Because the course might raise Leo’s pay, the loan is automatically good debt.
steps.explain: Good debt is cheap borrowing that builds your future. $520 of interest on $2,000, plus a shaky payment history, is worth a hard look.

steps.prompt: What is the careful move before Leo signs?
choices: Compare the total cost, and ask if a cheaper way to pay for the course exists
Sign today so the seat does not vanish
Let his cousin sign without reading
steps.explain: The monthly $105 is the easy number. The $2,520 is the real one.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Borrowing Basics
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: You borrow $5,000 and pay back $5,800. How much is interest?
Which one lets the lender take the car if the payments stop?
choices: Money a friend gave you as a gift
steps.explain: The car backs the loan. A typical card has no property behind it.

steps.prompt: A co-signer can be forced to pay the full remaining debt.
steps.explain: That is what the signature means.

steps.prompt: You have $300 left after needs. The payment would be $450. What is true?
choices: Lenders only offer payments you can afford
steps.explain: $450 is more than $300.
